n: This topic is devoted to forensic toxicology. Impairment of health and death from chemical factors are relatively common in the examination of dead bodies and living persons. Among violent deaths, poisonings rank third after mechanical injuries and mechanical asphyxia. Forensic toxicology resolves the tasks set by law-enforcement bodies. Remember: the science of forensic medicine began to take shape precisely from this direction.

t: The concept of poison and poisoning
n: The concept of poison is relative. A poison is a substance a small amount of which impairs health or leads to death. There is neither an absolute poison nor an absolutely harmless substance. According to Paracelsus, only the dose turns a substance into a medicine or a poison. Toxicology is divided into several branches: industrial, agricultural, military, food, domestic and forensic toxicology. The forensic branch fulfils the tasks of law enforcement.

Poisoning may be of three kinds: homicide, suicide or accident. Most cases are accidents, followed by suicide. Homicide by poisoning is seen rarely. Thus the order of frequency, from most to least, is accident, suicide and homicide. Some accidental poisonings are iatrogenic: the cause is an error in determining a drug dose or use of another substance in place of a drug.

The factors influencing poisoning fall into four groups: the toxic substance, the organism, the route of entry of the poison, and the external conditions at the time of exposure. In the toxic substance, chemical structure determines the property. For example, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide, though similar in structure, are not equally toxic. Quantity is also important: therapeutic, toxic and lethal doses are distinguished. The effects of a 3 % acetic acid solution and acetic essence cannot be compared.

t: The toxic substance: physical state, solubility, vehicle
n: Let us consider three properties of a toxic substance. The first is the physical state: gaseous substances act more strongly than liquids, and liquids more strongly than solids, because they pass quickly into the blood. The second is solubility. Barium sulphate does not dissolve in water, so it is used in radiography. Barium chloride is soluble and is a strong poison. Organophosphorus compounds dissolve in fat and are absorbed through the skin. The third is the vehicle: arsenic is potentiated in an alkaline medium, cyanides in an acid one. Heavy metals show cumulation.

Now the factors related to the organism. Body mass, age and pregnancy matter: children are more sensitive, and sensitivity rises in pregnancy. In diseases of the heart, liver and kidneys, resistance falls. The stomach contents may alter the action of a poison. Genetic features also play a role: low cholinesterase activity, G6PD deficiency, idiosyncrasy. Repeated exposure leads to tolerance, while in drug addiction and toxicomania a withdrawal syndrome is seen.

t: Route of entry and external conditions
n: Poison enters the body through the skin, mouth, airways, rectum and by injection. Its rapid and complete passage into the blood determines the effect. Substances absorbed through the mucosa of the airways, rectum and vagina bypass the liver and act more strongly. External conditions are also important. A closed, hot, humid environment predisposes to poisoning with alcohol and carbon monoxide. With hydrogen sulphide, a confined environment is dangerous, for example sewer wells.

Forensic diagnosis rests on evidence gathered in three stages. The first stage is inspection of the scene and review of medical records. Here attention is paid to foreign odours, medicine containers, syringes and vomit. The second stage is examination of the body. The third stage is laboratory investigation, which includes histological, forensic chemical, biochemical, pharmacological and other methods. That is, the conclusion rests not on a single stage but on the sum of all three.

Signs on the body help in suspecting the poison. With corrosive poisons there are traces of chemical burns and streaks around the mouth. The colour of the lividity also differs: pink in carbon monoxide, bright cherry-red in cyanides, brown with methaemoglobin formers, and yellowish with haemolytic poisons. Odour is also significant. With cyanides a bitter almond odour is noted, with acetic acid a pungent odour. In strychnine, rigor is rapid and strong, whereas with muscle relaxants it is weak.

In poisoning, forensic chemical, that is, toxicological examination is most often carried out: qualitative and quantitative. Samples are taken by the "three points" rule, that is, from the sites where the poison entered, acted and is eliminated: stomach contents, part of the liver, and urine with a whole kidney. If the source is unknown, one third of the brain, one quarter of a lung, one third of the liver with bile, a kidney, stomach contents, intestine and 100–200 ml of blood are taken. In deep putrefaction a 1.5–2.0 kg "average sample" is taken.

Toxicokinetics is the sum of the entry, distribution, metabolism and elimination of a poison. Biotransformation takes place mainly in the liver. On oxidation of organophosphorus compounds their toxicity rises, while on hydrolysis it falls. Some substances form more toxic products on oxidation. Methyl alcohol gives formaldehyde, ethyl alcohol gives acetaldehyde, and ethylene glycol gives oxalic acid. This means that in the body it may not be the poison itself but its altered form that is dangerous.

The distribution of a poison depends on its properties. Fat-soluble substances accumulate in the brain, liver and adipose tissue. Arsenic and lead accumulate in bone and hair. In elimination, volatile substances are excreted through the lungs, water-soluble ones through the kidneys, and heavy metals through the large intestine. Toxicodynamics distinguishes three actions: primary toxic, subsequent toxic and metatoxic. Acetic acid is given as an example: burn, haemolysis, toxic hepatitis and nephrosis.

Let us consider the forensic classification of poisons. The first group is mainly local-acting agents: acids, alkalis, hydrogen peroxide, formaldehyde, potassium permanganate and tincture of iodine. The second group is mainly general, that is, resorptive agents. These include destructive poisons: mercury, lead, zinc, arsenic, phosphorus. There are also blood poisons and functional poisons. Functional poisons are divided into those that paralyse, excite or depress the CNS, and those acting on the peripheral nervous system.

Poisoning with acids is relatively common, especially with acetic acid; in most cases it is a method of suicide. Free hydrogen ions dehydrate the tissue and coagulate protein. As a result, coagulative, that is, dry necrosis, eschar and acidosis develop. The lethal doses of concentrated acids are as follows: sulphuric and nitric acids 5–10 ml, hydrochloric acid 15–20 ml, acetic essence 20–40 ml, carbolic acid 10–30 ml.

With acids the signs on the body also differ. Around the mouth, sometimes on the neck, there are streaks of parchment-like hardness. The mucosa of the lips and mouth is hardened and grey. The gastric mucosa is brownish-black with sulphuric acid, yellowish with nitric acid, which is the xanthoproteic reaction, and brownish-grey with hydrochloric acid. Perforation is more frequent with sulphuric acid. With hydrochloric and acetic acid there is oedema of the larynx and lungs. With acetic acid haemolysis is marked and a pungent vinegar odour is noted.

Poisoning with alkalis is rare and occurs on accidental ingestion. Mainly potassium, sodium and ammonium hydroxides are involved. The lethal dose of potassium and sodium hydroxides is 10–15 g, and of ammonium hydroxide, that is, ammonia solution, 25–40 ml. In local action the proteins liquefy and alkali albuminates form; this is colliquative necrosis. The injured area is soft, swollen and slippery. The local effect of ammonium hydroxide is weaker, but after absorption it disturbs the respiratory centre. The body smells of ammonia.

t: Mercury compounds: signs in the oral cavity
n: Among mercury compounds, corrosive sublimate, that is, mercuric chloride, dissolves well in water and is regarded as a strong protoplasmic poison. On ingestion, burning in the mouth and a metallic taste are felt. In the body, mercurial stomatitis and gingivitis are found in the oral cavity: swelling, haemorrhages, ulcers with a grey floor, and a dirty-grey border at the gum margins. In the large intestine "sublimate dysentery" develops, and in the kidney "sublimate kidney". For the dentist, the signs in the oral cavity are especially important.

t: Physical factors: temperature and heat stroke
n: Now we move to physical factors, first temperature. Body temperature is 36–37 °C. When it is below 22–25 °C or above 43–44 °C, changes incompatible with life occur in the tissues. Heat stroke arises when a lot of heat is produced and little is lost. The main mechanism is haemodynamic disturbance, blood thickening and hypoxia. The protracted form consists of three periods. When body temperature exceeds 42–43 °C, death results from primary respiratory arrest.

A burn appears when the skin temperature exceeds 45–50 °C. The depth of a burn depends on the source, temperature and duration; 4 degrees are distinguished. First degree: erythema, 3–4 days. Second degree: blisters, 10–20 days, without scarring. Third degree: necrosis. Fourth degree: necrosis of muscle and bone, only from the action of flame. The area is assessed by the "rule of nines", Wallace, 1951: head and neck 9 %, front of the trunk 18 %. A third- to fourth-degree burn of more than 10 % is considered life-threatening.

t: Vitality of the action of flame
n: It is important to establish the vitality of the action of flame. If soot is present in the airways, oesophagus and stomach, the flame acted during life. With postmortem exposure carboxyhaemoglobin does not exceed 20 %, whereas with exposure during life it may reach 60 %. The "crow's foot" sign is found on the eyelids. On the body, the action of flame produces the "pugilistic attitude". These signs help to distinguish exposure during life from postmortem exposure.

t: Low temperature: general hypothermia and frostbite
n: Low temperature has two manifestations: general hypothermia and frostbite. In general hypothermia, when body temperature falls to +30…+28 °C, cortical function is disturbed. Death at +25…+22 °C most often results from primary respiratory arrest. Vishnevskiy spots are small haemorrhages in the gastric mucosa; they are found in 80–90 % and can be detected even 6–9 months after death. Frostbite is divided into degrees I–IV. Life-threatening are: more than 10 % in third to fourth degree, more than 15 % in third degree, more than 20 % in second degree.

Let us consider the main factors of electric current. Electrical injury accounts for 1–2.5 % of all injuries. The standard for safe voltage is 24 V; most deaths occur at 220–380 V. As to current strength, 50 mA threatens life, and at 100 mA most outcomes are fatal. A frequency of 40–60 Hz is extremely dangerous, while a frequency above 10000 Hz does not cause injury. In resistance, skin and bone are highest; moist skin and sweating increase the effect, and fatal cases are more frequent in summer.

In industry and the home, alternating current is mainly used, so most electrical injuries result from it. At voltages up to 500 V, alternating current is more dangerous than direct. At 500 V the danger is equal, and above it direct current is more dangerous. The effect of 120 V direct current equals that of 42 V alternating current. High-voltage current, that is, above 3000 V, is converted into heat by the electric arc. It produces a local burn, and death is uncommon.

The local effect of electric current is of two kinds. The electric mark appears at the point where current enters and leaves, and the local temperature reaches 120 °C. It is round or oval, firm, with raised edges and a deep centre. The colour of metallisation depends on the metal of the conductor; for detection, colour prints, the radiological method and emission spectrography are used. An electrical burn forms at high voltage, the temperature is above 120 °C, and it is painless. Its true width becomes evident after 2–3 weeks.

Barotrauma related to the effect of pressure is rare. Hydrostatic pressure at a depth of 10 m is 2 times atmospheric, and at 20 m, 3 times. With scuba, in 80 % of cases pulmonary barotrauma is seen, in 20 % drowning. In the body, air embolism confirms this. In decompression, that is, caisson disease, nitrogen bubbles obstruct the blood vessels. At low pressure at 18000 m, which is 6 kPa, tissue fluids "boil".

Ionising radiation causes radiation sickness. Its forms differ by dose: up to 10 Gy the bone marrow form, 10–20 Gy the intestinal form, 20–80 Gy the toxaemic form, and above 80 Gy the cerebral form. In acute radiation sickness, the primary reaction lasts up to 3–4 days, then comes a latent period of 2–4 weeks, after which the overt clinical period begins. Necrotic gingivitis, loosening and loss of teeth are found in the mouth.

t: Examination of living persons: situations and questions
n: Now the examination of living persons. In practice it is precisely these examinations that are carried out most often. They are ordered to determine bodily injuries, sexual conditions, sexual offences, state of health and age. In determining state of health, questions of simulation, dissimulation and aggravation are resolved. In bodily injuries, the type of injury, its location, instrument, mechanism, age and degree of severity are established.

Examination of state of health is ordered in several situations: when a person fails to appear, when determining the ability to take part in judicial and investigative actions, and when postponing execution of a sentence. It is also ordered when a prisoner refuses to work and in refusal of military service. The examination is usually carried out by a commission, with the participation of appropriate clinical specialists; sometimes inpatient investigation is necessary. The commission considers the likelihood of simulation, aggravation, dissimulation, artificial diseases and self-mutilation.

Simulation is the presenting by a healthy person of a non-existent illness as real. The simulator's complaints do not match the objective signs, he gives confused information on the history of the illness and presents treatment as ineffective. Aggravation is the exaggeration of the signs of an existing disease or trauma. Here the proportionality of subjective and objective signs is analysed. Both may be deliberate or pathological; the pathological type is usually a symptom of a nervous or mental illness.

Dissimulation is the opposite of simulation: deliberate concealment of a disease or pathological state. It occurs in situations where special demands are placed on health: among applicants to military schools, pilots, divers and drivers. In artificial diseases, methods that do not pose a serious threat to life are mainly used: swelling, tumour, abscess, phlegmon and dermatitis; these occur more often on the limbs. In simulation, aggravation and dissimulation the examination is carried out by a commission, often in inpatient conditions.

Bodily injuries under the Criminal Code are divided into three groups: grave, of moderate gravity and light. Grave injury includes danger to life, loss of ≥33 % of working capacity, loss of sight, speech, hearing or an organ, termination of pregnancy, mental disorder and irreparable disfigurement. In injury of moderate gravity, health is impaired for more than 21 days or 10–33 % of working capacity is lost. Light injuries are divided into short-term and ordinary light.

Let us once more bring together the classifying features of the degree of severity. In light injury, health is impaired for up to 6 days. In short-term light injury, the impairment lasts more than 6 days but not more than 21 days, or working capacity is lost up to 10 %. Forensic and clinical evaluation are not the same concept, and the results may not coincide. If there are several criteria, the degree is determined by the criterion corresponding to the more severe degree.

t: Danger to life and working capacity
n: Injuries dangerous to life include fractures of the skull base and vault, severe brain contusion, fractures of the cervical vertebrae, and wounds penetrating the cranial, thoracic and abdominal cavities. The fact that the threat to life was removed by medical aid does not prevent the injury being assessed as dangerous. For working capacity, only general working capacity is taken as the criterion. Impairment of more than 120 days is conventionally regarded as persistent loss.

Duration of impairment of health is the most frequently used criterion and is set in days on the basis of objective medical data. This period is not identical to the duration of anatomical healing or treatment. Failure to seek medical aid does not exclude impairment. A period prolonged by individual characteristics, late presentation or shortcomings in care is not taken into account. That is, the period is determined by the course proper to the injury itself.

t: Loss of organ function (tongue, sight, hearing)
n: Let us consider loss of organ function with examples. Absence of the whole or half of the tongue, together with loss of speech, means loss of more than one third of working capacity; this is grave bodily injury. If visual acuity in both eyes is 0.04 or lower, sight is considered lost. Loss of hearing in one ear is an injury of moderate gravity. Loss of the hand or foot is equated with loss of the arm or leg.

Among grave consequences there are also termination of pregnancy, mental disorder and disfigurement. Termination of pregnancy is counted only when a dead or non-viable infant is born, and is assessed with the participation of an obstetrician-gynaecologist. In mental disorder, a psychiatrist is included in the commission of experts; if a causal link exists, the injury is assessed as grave. Irreparable disfigurement does not disappear without surgical intervention. Its assessment is within the competence of the court, with the participation of clinical specialists.

The examination is conducted in compliance with the requirements of legislation. These are the Criminal Code, the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Civil Code, the Code of Civil Procedure, the Code of Administrative Offences, and the laws "On Protection of Citizens' Health" and "On Forensic Examination". The algorithm is as follows: circumstances of the event, medical records, interview of the person, inspection, additional investigations and drawing up the conclusion. Original medical records must be presented. The person who ordered the examination answers for their authenticity.

Let us consider the stage of interview and inspection. The person is identified by a document such as a passport; in sexual conditions two photographs are also needed. In the interview it is established when, where, by whom, with what, on which region and how many times the action was applied. At inspection, the shape, size, colour of the injury, contamination, and the edges, ends and floor of the wound are studied. Photography is carried out only with the person's permission.
